tagline: Battleground Road links Cowpens town with the preserved Revolutionary War battlefield.
intro: SC 110 runs 9.280 miles between Cowpens and Cowpens National Battlefield near Chesnee. Named Battleground Road throughout, it is a rural, two-lane highway with few intersections. Its signs designate it east–west, although the road physically runs north–south.

The highway number originally belonged to a different road: in 1936, SC 110 ran north from Chesnee to the North Carolina border. That stretch became part of US 221 in 1942, and SC 110 returned in 1949 on a route close to today’s. A slight westward rerouting followed in the mid-1950s.

For a southbound drive, start at SC 11 and US 221 Alternate beside the battlefield, then follow Battleground Road to US 29 in Cowpens. The battlefield preserves the site of Daniel Morgan’s victory over Banastre Tarleton on January 17, 1781; the town’s 1896 depot belongs to a later chapter of travel.

moments.title: Cowpens National Battlefield
moments.text: The cabin at Cowpens represents a later use of the battlefield: it is a reconstruction of Robert Scruggs’s log home, associated with farming before the park was established. The battlefield itself preserves the place where Daniel Morgan defeated British commander Banastre Tarleton on January 17, 1781. Federal commemoration began with Cowpens National Battlefield Site in 1929. The National Park Service unit includes battle interpretation and a walking tour of the field. The preserved battle site and reconstructed cabin tell different parts of the land’s history. A fiber-optic map in the visitor center explains the Southern Campaign and the battle.

moments.title: Cowpens
moments.text: Cattle pens near the original town site gave Cowpens its name. The town was chartered on February 20, 1880, and incorporated in 1900. The battlefield is a separate place, nine miles north in Cherokee County; Cowpens town lies in Spartanburg County. Its depot dates to 1896, during the years between charter and incorporation.

moments.title: Cowpens Depot
moments.text: Cowpens moved its depot one block off railroad property in 1982. Southern Railway had built the station in 1896; it closed in 1967. The building is a single-story wooden rectangle painted gray, with a gable roof and a platform for loading freight. Now also known as the Cowpens Depot Museum and Civic Center, it was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1997. An historic railroad car is displayed beside the relocated station.
